newsitem.title: JAPAN: Greenspan says Japan committed to financial reform.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan says Japan committed to financial reform.

text.p: U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday applauded Japan's "Big Bang" financial reform proposals and said he thought Tokyo was serious about putting its words into action.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week unveiled a five-year Big Bang plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001 in order to catch up with reforms carried out years ago in Europe and North America.
Some foreign business executives have expressed doubt about the vision being fully realised, but Greenspan was optimistic.

"I think the prime minister's and the finance minister's commitment to this strikes me as a very hopeful sign for the future and we in the Western financial centres are very strongly rooting for terrific competition coming from Tokyo," Greenspan told a news conference.
"I'm sure we will all rue the day when it comes, but it will be good for all of us," he said.

Greenspan, in Tokyo for two days of talks with Japanese financial and monetary authorities, also expressed scepticism about the idea of setting target zones for exchange rates, as advocated by some financial experts.
On Japan's reform plans, he said he was "somewhat surprised" by Japan's high degree of commitment to reform. "I must say, I suspect they will succeed," he added.
"I recognise that in the past there has been a degree of scepticism about these types of initiatives," Greenspan said.

"Things are changing here and I think the reason they are changing is a very increasing awareness that the underlying financial structure as it currently exists is not, in fact, at a sufficient level of competitiveness to match Tokyo with New York and London as key financial markets," he said.
Financial experts have said that many reform proposals, some under discussion for years, faced tough opposition from financial sectors expected to suffer most.
But business executives in Japan also believe Hashimoto and other policy-makers are convinced of the need to change or risk Japan's markets and economy falling further behind.
Greenspan said the United States and the rest of the world would benefit, not suffer, from Japanese financial reforms.

"...international finance is not a zero sum game. It is not that any particular advances in Tokyo are at the expense of New York or London or Frankfurt or anybody else, because there is a synergistic interaction which creates benefits to all of us."

Greenspan also said that successful Japanese Big Bang reform would boost the yen's role as an international currency, but not at the expense of the dollar or the new single European currency set to be introduced in 1999.

He said Japanese authorities were working to solve the problem of bad loans burdening the nation's financial system. "I don't think there is any reasonable expectation of concern now that the issue has been joined," he said.

Japan's banking system has been struggling with bad loans since the bursting of the late 1980s "bubble economy" of sky-high land and share prices. Most big banks are over the worst but smaller institutions still face difficulties.

Greenspan was cool towards the notion of target zones for foreign exchange rates as advocated by some experts, including economist Fred Bergsten, head of the Institute for International Economics in Washington.

"Until I see some evidence in a concrete manner that such types of ranges really do work, I would be sceptical," he said. "I would be inclined to say that the type of system we currently have probably is about as good as we're going to get, at least for the time being."
Greenspan was due to leave Japan later on Tuesday.
